  • In a recent development, I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs. More about Eric ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career. Now I want to share this knowledge with you.

Accessibility is a core part of a functional digital experience. As the LLM chat pattern continues to spread like wildfire across the web, we risk excluding people if these experiences are not built with accessibility as a core consideration.

It is also worth re-mentioning what “exclusion” means here: It’s the loss of knowledge, the loss of opportunity, the loss of utility, the loss of employability, the loss of entertainment, and more.

“Immersive LLM chat experience” is a catch-all term for full-screen experiences like Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, America.gov, Glean, and other similar websites and web apps:.

The majority of what this post covers applies to both web apps and native apps. This is because these experiences are typically built using web technologies, then placed in a native wrapper via frameworks such as Electron or Tauri.

Recent findings suggest that immersive LLM chat experiences are not patterns such as a pop-up chat, inline text generation utilities, or summarization tools. These simpler applications of LLM technology will have different considerations and expectations. Instead, this is a starting point for making those other experiences accessible.

Industry observers note that there is nothing special about chat-based UIs when viewed via the lens of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. They are interactive experiences, built using web technologies. The losses I’ve described — and the legal liability associated with them — are access barriers in the same way any other web content can be an access barrier.

I would also like to mention the social model of disability here: the idea that exclusion can be created by the built environment. For example, consider an elevated entryway that uses a gently sloping ramp in place of stairs.

Built environments also extend to digital experiences, and the social model also applies here. The main activities undertaken to operate an LLM chat are already well-established:.

It is how we facilitate — or fail to facilitate — those interactions that’s the salient bit.

Before we get into the technical aspects, we must consider the overwhelming visual bias that permeates software creation.

Industry observers note that we live in a highly visual culture, so our outputs unconsciously reflect and reinforce that. What we need to do here is be aware of and think through the non-visual considerations.

While not all disabilities are blindness or low vision conditions, a lot of the core interactions of an LLM chat do need specific accommodations for these two types of disability.

Sources indicate that recall the social model of disability here, and how it applies to the main flow of using an LLM-based chat. You:.

Let’s demonstrate at a high level what someone who can fully see the screen experiences compared to someone who uses a screen reader and cannot see the entire screen, or large portions of it:.

Visually, we can see the LLM reply appear. Someone who uses a screen reader does not know new content has appeared because:.

So, how do we create an experience for someone who uses a screen reader that is equivalent to the experience of someone who can fully see the screen? To start, we use live regions.

Live region announcements will enable someone to know what the LLM has responded with without having to move focus from the input used for prompting. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, glancing upwards to read the LLM response when it appears.

First, read this excellent article by TetraLogical if this is your first attempt at getting live region announcements working. They’re tricky to get right, and this article sets the record straight.

It has been revealed that one common pitfall I want to call specific attention to is applying aria-live on each LLM response message. Don’t do this. Instead, use a dedicated live region area to announce each message’s content.

The live region area should be placed at the end of the DOM and used for all live region messaging. This method is far more stable and reliable, which is notable for ensuring everyone understands what the experience is communicating.

With that established: What we want to do is trigger a live region announcement when the LLM’s chat reply reveals up in full on the screen.

This creates an outcome where you can read the message if you can see the screen, and hear or feel the message if you cannot.

There are a few things to do when creating a good user experience for the people who rely on these live region announcements. These considerations mean the difference between a compliant-yet-unusable outcome and something that genuinely works for the person using it.

Attempting to announce the message as it streams in may create a juddering and confusing experience that’s difficult for someone to parse.

It is better to wait until the message has completed streaming, and then announce the message’s content in full.

Responses from an LLM often take time to complete. Generally speaking, there are three ways to show a response is still processing:.

Sources indicate that these experiences are typically only shown visually. If you cannot see the screen, it may lead to it feeling like the experience has stalled or crashed — especially if the response is for a large or complicated request that takes a while to work through.

To address this, we’ll want to use live region announcements:.

In a recent development, if text is visually shown on the screen: Ensure a companion live region announcement is also triggered at the same time the loading message text is displayed. The text string for the live region announcement should be the same as what is shown visually, to be sure to ensure parity of experience:.

If a text-less loading animation is shown on the screen: Ensure the loading state is also communicated to assistive technology.

A live region announcement that mentions the reply is loading after a set amount of time will facilitate an equivalent experience for this interaction. It doesn’t have to be too verbose; the word “Loading” can suffice:.

Triggering the loading message five seconds after prompt submission seems to be the sweet spot, according to the inclusive user research I evaluated. You can then have your logic repeat the loading message every five seconds until the LLM completes its actual reply.

Recent findings suggest that be sure to also announce the reply immediately as it finishes streaming. You don’t need to wait until the next five-second loading message cycle is complete.

Industry observers note that also consider randomly selecting from a set of different phrases that communicate that a response is being formulated after the initial “Loading” message is dispatched. This helps in scenarios where someone may think the loading experience itself has crashed or stalled.

In a recent development, we’ll eventually be able to replace the technique TetraLogical outlined with ariaNotify(). It is a much-needed and welcome addition to the platform, and will drastically lower the hacks and headaches many developers encounter when creating and managing live region announcements.

Sources indicate that baseline lists the ariaNotify() method as having cross-browser availability at the time of this article’s publication. However, there are two factors to consider here:.

Also consider that while a polyfill for ariaNotify() is available, you need to factor in whether it has both:.

What this realistically means is holding off for a while on ariaNotify() in favor of the tried and true TetraLogical live region technique.

Headings are the most popular way people who use screen readers navigate around an experience. Because of this, I advocate for inserting visually-hidden headings before each chat message.

Here’s a simplified version of that in code:.

And here’s what the code might look like using the actual content from a human question and an LLM response:.

So, why the “You remarked:”/”Cody said:” prefix? Remember the visual bias. Visually, we can see the left- or right-hand alignment of messages, used to indicate who is saying what.

The prefix serves the same purpose: identifying the message’s owner. This allows people to quickly move through a conversation the same way someone might quickly scroll upwards to re-establish context, checking who remarked what and when.

Sources indicate that using landmark regions to wrap the larger overall areas of your LLM chat experience helps people understand its overall layout. It can also enable quick screen reader navigation to each area:.

Landmarks allow someone who cannot see the screen to learn about its overall makeup. This is the equivalent of how we promptly move our eyes and tilt our heads to different overall areas when scanning the screen to initially learn the overall layout of an experience.

I am hesitant to wrap chat messages in section or other landmark elements. The reason for this is that they “pollute” the list of landmarks a screen reader can generate, making navigation more laborious. This is especially relevant for long-running sessions where many messages are present.

Compare the following and ask yourself which one would be easier to move through with your keyboard if trying to jump from the prompt content area back to the sessions area:.

Here, our visually hidden heading elements serve as a dedicated navigation mechanism for moving through the LLM conversation.

In addition to headings and landmarks, there are two other ways to let people get around quickly:.

Skip links — sometimes referred to as skip navigation — allow you to swiftly jump to another area on the same page or view.

Skip to main content links are commonplace on many mature websites and web apps. Immersive LLM chat experiences should be no different.

Place a skip link in the DOM that allows someone to jump to the main conversation area before any other DOM content that is shown visually on the screen.

Also consider using additional skip links that enable:.

Composite widgets are used when a discrete section of content contains multiple interactive elements. Focus is then managed within this section by the developer, so that:.

For the purposes of an immersive LLM chat experience, we want to make conversation lists composite widgets. This enables someone to rapidly navigate both within and past the entire list.

Sources indicate that here, consider the use case of someone who exclusively relies on a keyboard to navigate. Compare pressing Tab 50 times to get through each of the 50 conversation sessions you’ve created versus pressing Tab once. Now consider motor control conditions where those keypresses can be fatiguing, or even painful to perform.

Once someone places focus on a conversation list composite widget, they can use the Up and Down arrow keys to navigate through each conversation session list item.

As a quality-of-life improvement, I also like to support the following keyboard interactions:.

To save you a lot of headaches and prototyping: Corner cases around focus management and usability expectations for people who rely exclusively on keyboards work against you if you try to go with a feed pattern approach.

According to recent reports, there’s no need to unnecessarily overcomplicate things. The article elements’ wrapping messages with visually-hidden headings approach that I’ve described earlier is both simple and effective.

Recent findings suggest that people who use assistive technology understand the simpler approach, and it involves far less effort to maintain. It’s a win-win!

It has been revealed that pressing F6/Shift+F6 to hop around different areas of the app is an older navigation technique some people who use Windows screen readers employ when navigating through installable desktop apps. Think of it a lot like navigating by landmark.

Recent findings suggest that LLM chat experiences are effectively apps in their own right. Because of this, we can recreate the F6 navigation experience and accommodate those who might attempt it. That means:.

There’s no secret sauce here. For starters, place an id on each landmark, as well as tabindex="-1". Also ensure each landmark other than main has an accessible name, granted via either aria-label or aria-labelledby.

According to recent reports, after that, have an event listener set up to recognize Control+F6 and Control+Shift+F6 key presses. Set focus to:.

Industry observers note that and voilà! We now have web-based F6 navigation.

As it is an older technique, people who are younger or less experienced with screen readers may not know F6 navigation exists.

According to recent reports, consider socializing the capability in the accessibility portion of your application’s settings menu to address this lack of awareness. Also consider exposing and making F6 navigation re-bindable as another discovery technique, provided your application supports keyboard shortcut rebinding.

Again, this advice only applies to an immersive LLM chat experience. Help agent popups and other less-sophisticated experiences have different expectations.

There are two areas that deserve more finesse when considering where to set focus when F6 navigation is used: the prompting input and the conversation.

Setting focus directly on the input used to type prompts — and not its parent form landmark element — allows someone to quickly get into the action.

Similarly, setting focus on the visually hidden heading of the last message displayed allows them to rapidly jump to the content the LLM generated — a data attribute such as data-last-message can be really helpful for managing this.

In a recent development, using F6 and Shift+F6 keypresses allows someone to hop from the chat input to what the LLM outputs, then back again. This enables rapid keyboard-based review and iteration on an LLM’s output.

Adjust the text size of your experience and double-check that content is not clipped, or that there’s horizontal overflow.

Industry observers note that people increase the text size of the experiences they use, and more than you’d probably guess. They also resize application windows. Also consider that most LLM-based chat designs tend to use a smaller text size to allow for more information shown on screen.

Because of these two factors, it makes sense to evaluate how your experience holds up when the browser font size is increased.

In a recent development, customization lives at the heart of accessibility. It’s only natural that LLM-based chat experiences have preferences to better accommodate all the different ways people use them.

In a recent development, in that vein, thoughtful preference offerings can go a long way to helping out people with access needs. Here are some that I’ve found to be particularly useful.

Sources indicate that some LLMs perform interim actions that are circumstantially less important than the messages they ultimately generate. Here, consider programming-oriented LLMs. They can perform actions like researching and reasoning, code search, and tool calls.

These secondary actions typically have a smaller, less visually important treatment compared to the messages that contain the main LLM response content. This is because the results are more important than the methodology when using this type of interaction.

Announcing each of these secondary actions could lead to a confusing or overwhelming experience, especially if multiple actions are clustered and fire off live messages in rapid succession.

According to recent reports, to address this, you can allow people to circumstantially switch off the announcements for this type of ancillary information. The content in the conversation is still present; it just isn’t announced via a live region. This is equivalent to how someone who can see the screen can skim over them.

Letting someone re-enable these types of announcements also grants parity in experience, in that it allows them to know the actions are happening if they want a more information-intensive experience. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, intentionally paying close attention to the LLM’s actions.

It might also be worth investigating letting people toggle visually hiding and showing these less vital announcements, as well. This can help people with attention or cognitive considerations, who may be less familiar with technical jargon.

Recent findings suggest that loading animations and large animated effects, like streaming conversations and side panels expanding and collapsing, can be distracting for some people with attention and cognitive considerations. That can go a long way toward breaking someone’s flow.

To address this, you can provide a toggle to turn off animations, reducing their transition time to zero.

You should also strive to be a respectful and courteous steward of the experience. Default your animation toggle to an off state if a request for a reduced motion experience has been in the device operating system. You can use the prefers-reduced-motion media feature to achieve this. Also consider a setting that can re-enable animation, even if a reduced motion request is present.

According to recent reports, some people can get distracted by, or have their focus disrupted by, sound effects. This is similar to animation considerations.

Recent findings suggest that letting people turn off app-specific sound effects means they don’t have to mute their entire device. Here, consider things like other apps playing flow state-inducing music or white noise that they might be using to help them focus.

Alternatives for sound-based notifications include, but are not limited to:.

I am of the school of thought that any experience that uses keyboard shortcuts also needs to allow both editing and being switched off, both in bulk and on a shortcut-by-shortcut basis.

You may be quick to think of conflicts with assistive technology, but I’d also like to take this space to remind you of different language keyboard layouts.

Live region messages are plain text strings. These strings are announced by screen readers in full in one go from start to end.

Recent findings suggest that semantic information that comes for free by using the appropriate HTML element isn’t present in live region announcements—it’s stripped out. Because of that, we need to think about how we could make our live region content both clear and useful.

Industry observers note that each type of special content has its own considerations. For my work, I created special cases for tables and blocks of code:.

Sources indicate that A table’s cell content will sound odd when declared without the companion semantic structure conferred by elements such as table, th, tr, and td. Relationships between columns and rows aren’t present in a live region announcement, either.

Because of this, we can convert the live region announcement of tables to use a concise description of the number of rows and columns, plus a general description and overall trends it might highlight.

A block of code sounds like gibberish when the line breaks are stripped away, and the content is flattened into a single string.

And if it’s a large block of code, it can be a tedious amount of gibberish to parse — nobody wants to sit through an announcement of 2,376 lines of code, painstakingly unveiled character-by-character.

To accommodate this, we can convert the live region announcement of code blocks to use the filename or file type, plus how many lines of code the block contains.

Also note here that people can revisit the actual message content itself. The actual message content will ideally have the appropriate semantics applied to it. This means things like tables being unveiled as, and navigated through as, table content.

It has been revealed that in this way, the live region message is a context-setting preview of what to expect. This is the equivalent of quickly visually skimming a message as it is streaming in, then scrolling back to review its content with more attention afterward.

According to recent reports, all of the previous is built atop feedback from testing different approaches and noting what works, and what could be improved. You want to facilitate disabled people being the experts in their own lived experience, and not treat others’ advice as the more credible source.

Inclusive user research is a vital way of determining if an experience is actually usable. Centering disabled people’s observations and perspectives is a way to take an experience beyond baseline compliance and create something usable and equitable.

It is vital to ensure that everyone can use chat-based LLM interactions as the pattern continues to proliferate. Although this is not an exhaustive list of everything you’ll need to do, the content above covers a wide swath of the main places accessibility barriers and friction may show up.

It is my sincerest hope that the improvements I’ve learned about and implemented can help you with your efforts to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who use assistive technology to get what they want or need online.

Thank you to Sarah Higley, whose research and efforts in this area informed key parts of this work.

Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party.
  • Industry observers note that hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions.
  • Hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party. With Orbán’s culturally regressive movement in tatters, Budapest is now reclaiming its status as one of Europe’s most important artistic capitals, and experiencing a wave of visitors newly drawn to the city in the wake of the country’s political about-face.

Industry observers note that hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions. The sprawling, multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary, which once stretched from the Mediterranean to what is now southwestern Ukraine, rebelled against Hapsburg dominance in the mid-19th century. That break culminated in 1866, when Austria and Hungary became constituent parts of a upcoming dual monarchy, spurring on the 1873 union of the separate towns of Buda and Pest, reconstituted as a Belle-Époque boomtown.

Hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility. The museum’s broad range of Old Master paintings and its world-class prints and drawings collection arguably make it the most crucial museum of its kind between Vienna and St. Petersburg. In 1957, the bulk of its Hungarian holdings were separated into a new institution, the Hungarian National Gallery, which eventually moved over to the Buda side of the city, into the onetime Habsburg Royal Palace. Though the Orbán regime had planned to rehouse it again, it remains in situ for the time being, and its collections of Hungarian art, spanning centuries, testifies to a rich and varied artistic tradition almost entirely unknown outside the country. Back over in Pest, a new cultural development, Müpa Budapest, opened in 2005, providing a home to the city’s Ludwig Museum, with a collection of contemporary art from national and international figures.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508)Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareTiny and technically unfinished, with the Virgin’s face and the figures of the Christ child and St. John the Baptist mere underdrawings, this tempera-and-oil on panel work has a grace and graphic quality that have helped make it the best-known Renaissance work in the country.

Produced at the end of Raphael’s Florentine period, when his output still reflects a youthful interest in Leonard da Vinci, the painting apparently first made its way north of the Alps in the early 18th century during the papacy of Clement XI, landing in the Esterházy collection by 1812. Stolen in 1983, along with the museum’s prized Giorgione portrait and other works, it was recovered the following year in a Greek monastery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870).

Credit: Museum of Fine Arts Budapest – Hungarian National Gallery.

Recent findings suggest that mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870)Hungarian National GallerySzent György térIn Hungary’s heyday before the First World War, when Budapest began to compete with Vienna, painter Mihály Munkácsy was a national hero. Born in what is now Ukraine, then educated at the art academies of Vienna, Munich and Düsseldorf, he eventually settled in Paris, with a base of collectors stretching from Central Europe to the American Midwest. His Budapest funeral procession, in spring 1900, was witnessed by hundreds of thousands people and remains a unique event in the history of the country.

Working in a number of established genres, from history painting to portraiture, he went on to decorate both Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum and Budapest’s upcoming Parliament building. But this breakthrough work—which scarcely gives a clue whether the condemned man in question is a criminal or a victim of injustice—remains his best known. Winning a gold medal at the 1870 Paris Salon, it was a main topic of conversation in the French capital during the final days of the doomed Second Empire.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareThe MFAB's prints and drawings collection has legendary status among scholars in the field, with key works stretching from Renaissance Italy to early 20th-century Vienna, leading up to the present day. This exquisite Leonardo drawing—one of three in the collection—is a preparatory work associated with a planned mural in Florence’s Palazzo Vecchio meant to commemorate the Florentine Republic’s victory over the Duchy of Milan in 1440.

Sources indicate that left unfinished in 1506, when Leonardo himself left for Milan, the partial mural, made using an unstable oil-based technique, was nonetheless one of Cinquecento Florence’s star attractions, until its degraded version fell victim to a 1560s renovation. This red-chalk drawing of a Florentine captain, produced using a live model, is known for its depiction of intense emotion.

Hungarian crown jewels on display in the parliament building.

Photo: Schopenhauer; Courtesy Wikimedia.

In a recent development, the Holy Crown of Hungary (around 12th century)Hungarian ParliamentKossuth Lajos térThe Kingdom of Hungary—defeated in the First World War, then dismantled, degraded and now disappeared—lives on in this mysterious and glorious object. One of Europe’s oldest surviving crowns, with a lower section of enamel imagery dating all the way back to medieval Byzantium, it likely took on its present appearance in the 12th century. Containing both Latin and Greek inscriptions, and bejeweled with sapphires, garnets and amethysts, the elaborate golden crown had mystical status. It was not only a symbol, but treated as the actual incarnation of the Hungarian state, and sovereigns were not regarded as rulers until it was placed on their heads.

A miraculous survivor of Hungary’s cataclysmic 20th century, it was brought back into use in 1990 following the collapse of communism. Placed on Hungary’s newly devised coat of arms, it has been on display in the national parliament since 2000.

Lili Ország’s Wall of Icons II (Blue) (1969).

Hungarian National GallerySzent György térNow regarded as one of the most crucial artists to emerge in Hungary after the Second World War, Ország, born into a Hungarian Jewish family in what is now Ukraine, barely escaped being deported to Auschwitz and later survived the war as a Christian convert.

According to recent reports, judaism, Christianity, and her own biography fuse together in her mature paintings, whose religious elements were in defiance of official communist policies. This late piece, showing a repeating Madonna-and-Child motif, is part of a series of oil-on-fiberboard works. Invoking her longstanding interest in Orthodox Christian imagery, it also alludes to her own trauma at not having had a child.

An apparent genre scene showing a rustic girl carrying food and water, the painting is in fact a wartime vision of desperate heroism. The late art critic Robert Hughes was fascinated by the work, which he regarded as an “emblem of resistance.” He writes, in his 2003 biography of the artist: “You would be very grateful to see her if you were crouched stiffly behind a rock in the parching autumn sun of Aragón, breathing hot dust with the ricochets whining above.”.

This installation on the banks of the Danube, which memorialises the victims of the predominantly anti-Semitic massacres by Hungary’s fascist militias in 1944-45, is now considered one of the most artistically successful.

Industry observers note that comprising 60 pairs of rusty iron shoes, it was devised by Togay, a filmmaker, and executed together with Pauer, a performance artist and sculptor. Fixed in concrete but eerily scattered, the shoes—in women’s, men’s, and children’s sizes and styles—recall the militia's orders of its victims to remove their shoes before shooting them into the river.

Their work is hard to find back in Budapest, but their near contemporary, Victor Vasarely, the great pioneer of Op Art, has his own museum here.

Recent findings suggest that schooled in Modernist trends in a Budapest private art academy, Vasarely decamped for Paris in 1930, and his experiments there in the late 1930s anticipated Op Art’s illusions and manipulations by some three decades. This tempera-on-paper work was a stand-out at this year's survey of the artist, Vasarely 120, held at MFAB. It is considered a great forerunner of the movement, which Vasarely went on to promote, often in ever-larger formats, until his death in 1997, aged 90.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leonardo Pertileâs book design for ADI Design Museumâs Compasso dâOro packs 1,040 pages into twin cloth volumes set in OT Marmo.

Compressing nearly seventy years of Italian industrial design into a 1,040-page brick isnât a subtle problem. Presented by Fondazione ADI, ADI Associazione per il Disegno Industriale, and ADI Design Museum, this Treccani monograph is edited by Beppe Finessi and designed by Leonardo Pertile as twin cloth editions. Brick-red cloth printed in royal blue marks the English Historical Collection with a yellow ribbon, while yellow cloth inked in red identifies the Italian Collezione Storica with a navy ribbon. Neither cover uses product photography. A large blind-debossed compass presses into the woven board under Omnitypeâs pre-release OT Marmo capitals, and opening the red cover flashes yellow endpaper beside three tall floor lamps.

According to the museumâs notes, the publication holds 2,275 images across three parts: ADI Design Museumâs archival role, the 1954â2022 Compasso dâOro Roll of Honour, and critical essays and interviews. Pertile keeps that scale legible by shifting the grid per section so the book design doesnât lose its rhythm. On pages 154 and 155, Anty Panseraâs essay wraps justified columns around four staggered black-and-white ceremony photos. Another spread runs a hand-drawn nebido logo study on millimeter graph paper across the top above justified prose and hanging-indent captions citing Franco Albini, Franca Helg, and Bob Noorda. Turn to pages 474 and 475 for Anno 1967 and the density jumps â Enzo Mariâs concentric Freud Opere sketches and Mario Piazzaâs ruled pull quote face Olivettiâs tight vertical matrix of color-coded marks.

Heavy catalogs donât work without quiet spreads. Page 577 pairs an overhead photo of a terracotta sofa and dark-green chaise directly above twin framed floor plans, leaving the plate clear of clutter. That open air widens in the essays and interviews. Alberto Saibeneâs Milano, 1954: cultura e industria opener floats OT Marmo headings high in white space above two narrow columns. On page 967, Beppe Finessiâs interview with Paola Antonelli switches to ragged-right text with outdented BF and PA initials in the margin so speakers scan fast. Itâs disciplined book design that makes a 1,040-page institutional archive easy to open and read.

  • A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

In a recent development, rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

Every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

Recent findings suggest that an AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

We can call that the break-even line. Returns to consumers come in three forms:.

In a recent development, for example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool indicates the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

Four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

These questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

Run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the glitch alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

According to recent reports, count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

Recent findings suggest that A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom says to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

In a recent development, you can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

Who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

Industry observers note that compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

For example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

Sources indicate that the nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

Industry observers note that every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

According to recent reports, error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

In a recent development, automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, customers stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

Sources indicate that map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

Show users where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

Recent findings suggest that letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

In a recent development, still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

According to recent reports, research in radiology shows how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result demonstrated how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

Question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

Industry observers note that ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

Sources indicate that table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

Put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

It has been revealed that let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

It has been revealed that question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

Question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

Question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

It has been revealed that on Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

Question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

According to recent reports, A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

The feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

According to recent reports, two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

Recent findings suggest that everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that latest capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

Audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

Start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that users might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

The attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1442 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November.
  • The mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for big works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses.
  • It has been revealed that for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers remarked that a date clash with Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to most local exhibitors selling around half, rather than all their stands.

The mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for big works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).

It has been revealed that for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” mentioned Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand—including photographs by the Kolkata-based filmmaker Ronny Sen referencing post-humanism—and rehung around 50% of it.

According to recent reports, notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a latest buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.

In the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.

Subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send out PDFs to its clients prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” remarked the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.

Art Mumbai takes place at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse.

With India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox remarked this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.

Also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that highlighted at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (New York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).

Sources indicate that several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. On the closing day, gallery director Ellie Harrison-Read said that she had a "good fair, but closing a few more sales could make it great”.

In a recent development, by and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works struggled. Niru Ratnam, which showed small paintings in muted palettes by the late Bengali-British Modernist Amal Ghosh and the British Indian Bhajan Hunjan, did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Ghosh to cover stand and shipping costs.

According to recent reports, while both Ghosh and Hunjan are increasingly being reappraised by world leading institutions such as Tate, they are relatively unknown figures in both the UK and India and have proved a tough sell in Mumbai. As one local dealer noted, "I rarely meet collectors here who lead with curiosity or instinct".

Another litmus test for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff remarked she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.

According to recent reports, the gallery did however sell to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art a $16,000 painting installation by Divya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff said.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of Picasso, a 1930s painting by the Spanish master was offered by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery revealed a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, gallery director Hugo Cobb decided to double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he stated.

The gallery did not sell the Picasso by the end of the fair, with Cobb attesting to the fact that the very top end of the Indian market still amounts to a handful of collectors. "There are maybe four or five collectors in this country who would buy it, and none of them did." The gallery did, however, sell a monumentally scaled Yoan Capote painting, embedded with fishhooks, for $1m to a local collector. Cobb added that should the gallery return to Art Mumbai, it will focus on bringing high value secondary market material.

As many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes remain local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by familiarity," says the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff.".

Recent findings suggest that further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes involved in shipping works in and out of the country. As the Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan said, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in art. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".

Meanwhile, issues of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one adviser, speaking anonymously, noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".

It has been revealed that india's art market growth indeed appears to be a domestic success story. This is in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.

While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, many collectors covet international—usually Western—names at the expense of local talent, India overwhelmingly supports its own artists: representatives from a growing number of new Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.

While India might not yet be ready for a truly international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which should help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer period.

AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

📅 2026-11-17 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

Lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

We asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most remarked they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

Recent findings suggest that these results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

Sources indicate that accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

In a recent development, this matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

So how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

Here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge shows up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

In a recent development, A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only shows correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

And it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize problems. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

Recent findings suggest that not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

Pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

How many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

As AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding challenges, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing new gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

Found the concern? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When issues end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

Every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the problem comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

According to recent reports, A passing test reveals a known matter hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

It has been revealed that we’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model

  • In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Organisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

It has been revealed that the campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

It has been revealed that for soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

According to recent reports, those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

Recent findings suggest that and yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

“Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”.

According to recent reports, according to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch says the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

Industry observers note that “Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch indicates. She plans to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Sources indicate that still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

The “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

Sources indicate that as of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

It has been revealed that beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto says, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

For the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto says, “that would be a huge victory.”.
