📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s New York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

Recent findings suggest that but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in Upcoming York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

Recent findings suggest that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across Upcoming York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s unveiled that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

According to recent reports, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's.

In a recent development, estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Acquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

According to recent reports, soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s Latest York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

It has been revealed that the subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

Recent findings suggest that the top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

According to recent reports, harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's.

Industry observers note that one of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

Industry observers note that mary Cassatt also established a upcoming auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

Industry observers note that only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giga rebuilds AD Italia for its 45th anniversary: the AD Italia redesign pairs Arizona type, Ghirri colour and a modernist grid.

Recent findings suggest that the first thing you see is the masthead. AD sits in black flared serif on a soft pink field, the letters drawn wide enough to carry the cover on their own, and the same confidence runs through the glitch. Inside, the November pages open on a white field with SPAZI set large in the same face, issue N.530, and the spreads that follow give each photograph a full page of air. The palette stays soft and everyday: coral, pale green and pale blue, the colours of an Italian landscape rather than a brand manual.

Recent findings suggest that proportion went to the type. Arizona, by Dinamo Typefaces, is almost a sans with flared strokes, and it brings the measure of Roman inscriptions to the page. A specimen page sets names in Arizona Flare Light, one per line, with nothing else on the field, and the same face carries the cover lines: SPAZI across a white cover, LA NOSTRA GUIDA AL SALONE 2025 stacked in white on black. The letters do the talking, and the layout stays out of their way.

According to recent reports, essentiality went to the grid. Giga built it on the logic of modern art catalogues: photographs get room of their own, captions stay small and precise, and the editorial pages stand apart from the advertising around them. A spread on David Bowie runs green panels beside a column of text that starts in 1972, when Bowie became Ziggy Stardust, and a grid of anniversary spreads collects 45 icons from the magazine's history on a single page.

Colour went to Luigi Ghirri. The case page sets the palette beside three everyday Italian landscapes, a canal road, green houses against the sea, a beach with swings, all in the soft register of Ghirri's photographs. The system names its colours plainly: PMS 2344 C coral, PMS 2260 C pale green, PMS 290 C pale blue, each with its hex code printed beside it, the way a printer would want it.

Wit went to the rhythm. Like Ettore Sottsass's Carlton bookcase, which slants its shelves and still holds books, the system plays with its own conventions, varying titles and images from story to story. The redesign released with the November 2026 matter and a room at PAC Milano built around one line: perfect proportions, essential function, a joke, the colours of every day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several new galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.

In a recent development, several notable artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The upcoming Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.

Industry observers note that the reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the newly introduced government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are prepares afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an notable moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.

According to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.

A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while latest ones been announced. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.

Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has announced that a upcoming museum will open in the former Presidential Palace in Babylon Photo: Hadani Ditmars.

Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.

It has been revealed that al-Dakhili has also revealed that the openings of three latest museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement states.

Alaska Mileage Initiative is one of the most valuable frequent flyer programs in the world despite being a relatively small airline. This creates structural pricing inefficiencies — especially on premium cabin routes to Asia and Oceania — that savvy travelers can exploit. Here's the insight that transforms this from "interesting" to "actionable": Alaska Airlines Mileage Strategy uses a fixed partner award chart, and that chart prices Cathay Pacific Business Class to Australia at 55,000 miles one-way — a number that hasn't kept pace with the explosive cash price inflation of premium cabin fares.

Most major U.S. loyalty programs have migrated to dynamic pricing, where award costs fluctuate with cash fare demand. Alaska hasn't done this for partner awards. Their chart is fixed. That means when Cathay Pacific's cash fares spike to $12,000 during Australian school holidays or peak summer travel, your award cost stays exactly where it was: 55,000 miles. After three days exploring Hong Kong, you reboard for the six-hour SYD leg, arriving in Sydney ready — genuinely ready, not depleted — to start your adventure.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

The single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who claims "I'm not seeing anything.".

It has been revealed that don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

Sources indicate that this is the most common and most painful mistake. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers are generally not reversible. If you transfer 165,000 Bonvoy points to Alaska and then discover no award space exists on your dates, you're stuck with miles you may not use optimally. Always confirm availability on ba.com before initiating any transfer.

It has been revealed that book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

Industry observers note that if Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. Qantas' "The Business" product on their A380 Sydney routes is exceptional in its own right — and availability patterns differ from Cathay, so checking both genuinely doubles your options.

Sources indicate that this redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

Minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Initiative miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

Within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy® credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

Recent findings suggest that this redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy® conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

It has been revealed that the fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy® points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

In a recent development, yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear promptly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

In a recent development, the Alaska Mileage Strategy redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.
  • Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.
  • It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Lv Xiaobin.

Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.

It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

According to recent reports, “But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the fresh one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.

“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”.

Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.

“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” stated Shisuo Design Office.

“Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio mentioned.

Sources indicate that externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio stated deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.

It has a rectangular plan, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.

Sources indicate that inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.

According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.

“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” noted the studio.

Recent findings suggest that “For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”.

Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.

Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

Photography by Lv Xiaobin.

Industry News: Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design indicates innovation lead

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers.
  • “I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon.
  • Sources indicate that tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Nike.

In a recent development, sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

“I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”.

Sources indicate that tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” noted McCartney.

“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”.

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

Industry observers note that “At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” stated McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”.

“If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”.

According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

Sources indicate that “It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” said McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”.

“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

Sources indicate that “So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “.

Recent findings suggest that while the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

It has been revealed that “There’ll be a few modifications,” he said. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.

“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”.

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “important part of the design and important part of this platform”.

The midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.

In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

“There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”.

“We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” said McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”.

Photography courtesy of Nike.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.
  • The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.

In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.

Alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, says: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a latest national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”.

Artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, claims the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.

In a recent development, charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he indicates. “The biggest issue seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”.

In a recent development, the CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report states.

Sources indicate that UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”.

Sources indicate that kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, says: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.

Industry observers note that “Focused giving” may be partly the answer says the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a new Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

pen.dev pairs a 60fps WebGL canvas and live shaders with browser import and two-way MCP integration for real product design.

We've been testing pen.dev closely for quite some time, and we're ready to say it: for our daily work at Abduzeedo, it has gotten our full attention and replaced Figma in our day-to-day flow. That isn't a claim we make lightly. pen.dev feels like the closest we get to designing the real product. For anyone who spends a lot of time in the browser inspector or has been coding in the past, the whole environment feels immediately familiar.

The speed is truly impressive, and that speed helps you ideate more. Built on a custom WebGL renderer, the canvas stays locked at 60fps even when you throw 10,000 photos and 10GB of content at it. Panning, zooming, and nudging dense artboards feel instant, with none of the sluggishness that slows down exploration.

What makes pen.dev feel like a real design tool rather than a prompt box is how much hands-on visual control you keep. You get a proper pen tool, flex layout, variables, snapping, and familiar shortcuts, alongside components with overrides and slots plus shared design systems that make it easy to manage your workflows and keep every project in sync across files. Real-time shaders, linear, radial, angular, and mesh gradients, and masking sit right inside the inspector. Having live shaders built directly into the canvas changes how rapidly you can test atmosphere and depth without jumping to another app.

Iterating with multiple agents is where the workflow really opens up. Instead of waiting on one linear prompt thread, you can spin up parallel agents to generate side-by-side variants right on the canvas and test completely different concepts at the same time. In the Goodies view, you can see directions like Darkmatter, Brickworks, and Verdant Ark laid out next to each other as real, editable frames. Agents can also draw custom icons and illustrations directly on the same layers you edit by hand, leaving plenty of room for the happy accidents that only happen when you're moving rectangles around yourself.

Recent findings suggest that one of our favorite features is importing directly from the browser. In the age of AI, design more than ever is a two-way street. Sometimes you don't start from the design tool at all, you start from a working prototype or a live site. Being able to pull that straight into pen.dev for quick visual iterations is often way quicker and cheaper than trying to explain every tweak to an AI in words. For those of us who sometimes have a hard time translating ideas into prompts, but not into visuals, that completes the loop.

You can also pull 10 to 15 live reference sites onto the canvas in a grid, or keep your running localhost app open in a split-screen browser right beside its source design to compare spacing and typography in real time.

Where things really click for us is the two-way MCP integration. Inside the settings panel, you can wire up external MCP servers like Linear, Notion, or Mobbin so agents on the canvas pull real product specs and UI references as you design. Going the other way, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Antigravity connect to pen.dev over MCP to read your frames directly.

Recent findings suggest that because every project saves as an open .pen JSON file right inside your repository, coding agents build from your actual components, spacing, and variables instead of guessing from a flat screenshot. You can open the design and code side by side with the VS Code and Cursor extensions, run headless workflows through the pen.dev CLI, or use one-click export to HTML with CSS or Tailwind.

It has been revealed that design thinking stays on the canvas, and clean implementation follows right behind it. Explore the tool and try the web app at pen.dev.

Recent findings suggest that smallRig’s Black Friday Sale just went live. According to recent reports, the tripods SmallRig developed with Potato Jet lead the sale list, and they are designed around fast setup. Squeezing a single lever, which SmallRig calls the X-Clutch, releases all three legs at once, and the tech giant says they extend and lock in about one second. Recent findings suggest that the SmallRig x Potato Jet TRIBEX SE is the less expensive of the two and is 30% off. It is $279.99 instead of $399.99, a saving of $120. The aluminum tripod weighs 8.2 pounds, extends from 9.1 to 65 inches, and comes with a fluid head, a tripod head that uses damping to smooth pans and tilts for video. The head carries up to 13.2 pounds, and SmallRig lists weddings, interviews, landscapes, and sports among its uses.

Its fluid head has a four-step counterbalance, a setting that keeps a tilted camera from tipping forward or back, and adjustable damping for pans and tilts. The quick-release plate locks in without being lined up first, and SmallRig claims the head also accepts the quick-release plates from DJI RS gimbals, which are motorized stabilizers, so a camera can go from stabilizer to tripod without a plate change.

At the other end of the price range, the CT-10 is also 30% off: $48.93, down from $69.90. The aluminum tripod has a ball head, which lets the camera tilt in any direction and then lock. It extends from 16 to 71 inches, folds to 16.9 inches, and converts to a monopod, a single-leg support. SmallRig describes it as a companion for hiking and travel, and the center column can be flipped upside down to put the camera near the ground for low angles and close-ups.

Industry observers note that A less expensive video option, the AD-01, drops from $159.99 to $119.99, a 25% discount. Its fluid head is rated for 17 pounds and the legs reach 73 inches. It has been revealed that the 73.4-inch heavy-duty carbon fiber video tripod is built for heavier rigs. SmallRig says the legs weigh 6.6 pounds and hold 66 pounds, and it rates the fluid head for 17.6 pounds. The tripod folds to 29 inches. It is $339.99, down 15% from $399.99.

A ball head suits stills. The two with heads rated for 11 pounds have a one-button lift and lock that SmallRig says sets the height with one hand. The 65.6-inch model with a ball head is $159.99, down 20% from $199.99. The 68.9-inch video model with a fluid head is 24% off at $303.99, from $399.99.

Industry observers note that the two 67-inch SmallRig x Potato Jet TRIBEX PRO monopods carry more and use the same X-Clutch as the tripods, with a pedal at the base that switches between free panning and a locked position with a tap of the foot. Each is $365.49, down 15% from $429.99. The fluid head version carries 13.2 pounds and is made for video. The ball head version carries 26.4 pounds, and SmallRig states it is suited to heavy telephoto lenses and full-frame cameras.

It has been revealed that two 99Wh V-mount batteries are in the sale. V-mount is the wedge-shaped battery mount used on many cinema cameras, monitors, and lights, and 99Wh, or watt-hours, is the amount of energy the battery stores. The number matters for travel: SmallRig says both batteries, at under 100Wh, meet the TSA’s requirement for carry-on bags.

The X99 is the one for people who want to see what every port is doing. It measures 4.9 by 3.1 by 2.7 inches, weighs 31 ounces, and is $209.99, down from $279.99. The T99 has seven ports and a rear light that helps with mounting it in dim rooms, and it costs less at $187.49, down from $249.99. Both are 25% off, and SmallRig says both recharge in two hours with 100-watt fast charging.

SmallRig rates both batteries IP54, a standard for resistance to dust and splashing water, and lists a drop rating of 4.9 feet for the X99 and 5.9 feet for the T99.

It has been revealed that the Nano36 and Nano72 are mini power banks with USB-C output. Both also have a 27.6-inch USB-C cable that retracts into the body. The 10,000mAh Nano36 delivers up to 45 watts and is $47.19, reduced from $58.99. The 20,000mAh Nano72 delivers up to 100 watts and is $63.99, reduced from $79.99. Both are 20% off. Check the connection and power requirements of the camera, monitor, or light before choosing any of the four.

The two RC lights in the sale are COB video lights. COB, short for chip-on-board, means the LEDs are packed into one small, bright source. Both are about 4.5 inches long and adjust from a warm 2700K to a cool 6500K.

The RC 100B is a 100-watt light with a built-in plate that accepts a V-mount battery, so it can run away from a wall outlet, and it can also be powered over USB-C. SmallRig puts its fan noise at about 26 decibels within 1 meter and says that is quiet enough not to disturb a recording. It is $183.99, down 20% from $229.99. The model on sale is the Standard Version, which does not include a battery.

Sources indicate that the RC 60B, sold here as the Mobile Version, has a built-in battery. SmallRig says it runs for 45 minutes at full power or 75 minutes in its eco mode and keeps working while it charges. It has a 63-watt maximum and comes with a grip handle, a light stand adapter, and a carrying bag. It is $169.15, reduced 15% from $199.

Recent findings suggest that the FL-90 is a 35.4-inch lantern softbox, a globe-shaped diffuser that spreads soft, even light, and it is $60.79, down 20% from $75.99. SmallRig notes it opens and collapses in one step. It weighs 1.85 pounds and comes with a skirt that controls where the light spills and a storage bag. It attaches to lights with a Bowens mount, a bayonet fitting common on studio lights. The RC 100B and RC 60B do not have that mount, and SmallRig’s listings say they need the tech giant’s Bowens mount adapter, sold separately, to use a softbox like this one.

Two lights are aimed at close-up work. The RM 03 is a bendable light for macro, or close-up, photography that SmallRig designed for subjects such as mushrooms, plants, and insects. It can wrap around a tree trunk, attach with its clamp, or stand on ground stakes, and it is rated IP54 against rain and dust. It is $39.99, down from $49.99. The RM01 kit is a 2.2-ounce light that SmallRig rates as waterproof. It comes with eight color filters, a diffuser, and a barn door, a set of flaps that narrows the beam. SmallRig suggests it for toy photography, stop motion, and macro. It is $31.99, down from $39.99. Both are 20% off.

Recent findings suggest that three zoomable flashlights are built to put colored or patterned light on a subject or a background. Each comes with gobos, patterned inserts that shape the beam. The RF 05B produces white light that adjusts from a warm 1900K to a cool 8000K. It weighs 7.6 ounces, is rated IP65 against rain and dust, and costs $31.99, down 20% from $39.99. The 10-watt RF 10C has LEDs in four colors (orange, blue, white, and red) and runs about three hours at full power, according to SmallRig. It drops to $39.99 from $49.99, also 20% off. The 20-watt RF 20C has five colors, and SmallRig suggests it for background and rim lighting, a light from behind that outlines the subject, in portraits at weddings and conventions. It is $67.99, down 15% from $79.99.

Sources indicate that the universal phone cage kit, a frame with two side handles for handheld filming, is $47.99, reduced 20% from $59.99. SmallRig notes the two handles add stability for moving shots, and the aluminum cage has mounting points for a microphone and a light. The All-in-One kit comes with an LED light and a microphone, plus a tripod and a power bank holder, and its handles rotate from the sides to the top. SmallRig says it fits phones from 2.52 to 3.46 inches wide. It is $161.49, down 15% from $189.99.

Recent findings suggest that the selfie monitor kit lets someone filming alone see the frame while using the phone’s rear camera. Its small monitor mirrors the phone’s screen wirelessly from up to 32.8 feet, and a wireless remote triggers the camera. It is $51.99, a 20% discount from $64.99. Read the listing before ordering: SmallRig notes the kit is not suitable for Google Pixel phones or the Samsung S22 series, and that with the iPhone’s own camera app it supports 1080p at 60 frames per second, not 4K at 60.

For filters, the 5-in-1 magnetic 67mm kit is $95.99, down 20% from $119.99. Its three filters attach magnetically, so they swap quickly: a variable ND filter, which darkens the image by an adjustable amount; a circular polarizer, which cuts glare and reflections; and a Black Mist 1/4 filter, which softens highlights. The kit also includes a threaded ring that puts the same filters on a camera lens with a 67mm filter thread. On a phone it needs one of SmallRig’s phone cages and a filter ring that is sold separately, so check the listing for the cage models it fits.

Recent findings suggest that smallRig’s Cage for DJI Osmo Action 6 (Advanced Edition) is a 2.4-ounce aluminum frame with a cold shoe, a slot for mounting a small light or microphone. Four accessories for DJI’s Osmo Pocket cameras are discounted, and fit differs by model. The auto-deploy mini tripod has the lowest price on the list at $14.44, 15% off $16.99. Its legs open on their own when it is set down, and they are magnetic. SmallRig notes they can hold up to 0.66 pounds on a refrigerator or another surface a magnet sticks to. The magnetic desktop stand tilts and has a magnetic back, a cold shoe, and a plate that fits Arca-type tripod clamps, a common quick-release standard. It is $27.99, down 20% from $34.99. SmallRig lists both for the Pocket 4P, Pocket 4, and Pocket 3. The variable ND kit is $33.14, reduced 15% from $38.99. ND, or neutral density, filters cut the light reaching the sensor so video can keep a slower shutter speed in bright conditions. The first kit has three fixed strengths that cut four, six, and eight stops of light, and each stop halves the light. The variable filter adjusts from one to five stops for changing conditions. SmallRig says neither kit interferes with the gimbal’s rotation or darkens the corners of the frame.

A cage is a metal frame that wraps a camera body and adds threaded holes for handles, monitors, and microphones. Each is built for one camera model, so match the model name on the listing to the camera.

In a recent development, for the Sony FX5, four HawkLock cages and kits are 20% off. The cage on its own is $71.99, down from $89.99, and has a clamp that keeps an HDMI cable from pulling out of the camera. The Advanced HawkLock cage is $95.99, down from $119.99, and SmallRig says its base slides straight into Arca-type tripod clamps and the DJI RS gimbals named on the listing, for quick moves between tripod, gimbal, and handheld shooting.

The SmallRig S70 Ultra-Thin Wireless Microphone has the deepest discount in the sale: 40% off at $53.99, down from $89.99, a saving of $36. SmallRig designed it for content creators, vloggers, and filmmakers who want to record audio without a bulky microphone setup, and indicates its thin, discreet design suits interviews, talking-head videos, and on-the-go recording, where keeping the microphone out of sight matters.

The prices in this article are the ones SmallRig supplied for Amazon U.S., and the other two stores may differ. Heipi’s Hybrid Tripod Head Promptly Swaps Between Ball, Fluid, and Gimbal Head Modes

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (401 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that with more creators capturing both photos and videos, accessory makers are stepping up to meet the demand.
  • Sources indicate that photographers often like ball heads because they are versatile, easy to adjust, and stable.
  • “Today, the line between photography and videography is becoming increasingly blurred.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with more creators capturing both photos and videos, accessory makers are stepping up to meet the demand. Heipi’s new 2-in-1 hybrid tripod head for photo and video promises the best of both worlds.

Sources indicate that photographers often like ball heads because they are versatile, easy to adjust, and stable. By loosening the head, photographers can promptly recompose their shots. However, ball heads are not as easy to control or as smooth for panning motion as a traditional pan-tilt fluid head, which videographers typically prefer. Further, Heipi says its new head also delivers the balancing performance of a gimbal head, a popular choice for wildlife and birding photographers with huge, heavy lenses.

“Today, the line between photography and videography is becoming increasingly blurred. During a single shoot, creators may switch between wide-angle and telephoto lenses, move from still photography to video, and capture a wider range of perspectives and moments,” Heipi writes on Kickstarter. “Yet different shooting needs often call for different support equipment: a ball head, a gimbal head, a fluid head, and more. Carrying multiple heads adds bulk to your gear and extra weight to every journey.”.

Heipi believes its latest hybrid head offers all the benefits of separate tripod heads in a single package.

The Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head weighs 560 grams (just over 1.2 pounds) and is about the size of a traditional ball head. However, it can instantly switch from ball head mode to pan-tilt mode, and videographers can screw on a grip for even more control.

Heipi’s latest tripod head also features a stepless counterbalance system designed for gear weighing from 1.5 to 5 kilograms (3.3 to 11 pounds). That encompasses a wide range of equipment, including those significant, heavy supertelephoto lenses mentioned earlier.

Recent findings suggest that the KB50 features a standard 3/8″-16 UNC female thread on its base, allowing it to attach to a wide variety of tripod legs. It also includes an Arca-Swiss clamp.

The Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head is available to back on Kickstarter now, starting at $428, which is a $120 discount compared to the $548 MSRP. Heipi notes it will begin shipping in April 2027. With just over 40 days left in the campaign, Heipi has already shattered its $10,000 goal.

#125949. Latest Update: The Associated Press is Moving Eight US Photo Editor Jobs to India

Latest Update: The Associated Press is Moving Eight US Photo Editor Jobs to India

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Associated Press is moving eight photo editor positions to India today, in a move condemned by unions.
  • In a recent development, the roles are currently carried out in the United States, but today is their last day.
  • “AP is at it again,” the AP News Guild wrote on X last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Associated Press is moving eight photo editor positions to India today, in a move condemned by unions.

In a recent development, the roles are currently carried out in the United States, but today is their last day. The offshoring follows similar moves this summer, when AP laid off 20 video production jobs in the U.S. and moved them to its hub in Noida, India.

“AP is at it again,” the AP News Guild wrote on X last week. “The News Media Guild learned Monday that AP will offshore eight photo positions after already gutting its U.S. video production team.”.

In a statement, the News Media Guild president Kimberlee Krusei called AP’s move “union busting.”.

“Fewer people, fewer communities being covered, and less news. That’s the impact of today’s decision,” states Krusei. “AP’s newsgathering has gone beyond ‘lean’ to leaving many coverage areas abandoned. The remaining journalists are asked to do the impossible and it demonstrates.”.

The Guild states that far from just picking photos taken by AP photographers, the editors provide direction, guide the photographers, correct essential information, and scrutinize images for alterations.

Sources indicate that “They bring decades of local knowledge, news judgment and connections. They negotiate with outside photographers to buy the rights to photos — a now essential part of covering breaking news.”.

One of the affected photo editors, Pablo Salinas, who is based in Newly introduced York, notes that he went above and beyond in 2019 when he obtained the rights to a shocking photo of a drowned father and daughter lying face down in the Rio Grande River.

Recent findings suggest that “That was a picture that I don’t think any other photo editor would have been able to get,” indicates Salinas. “Because it wasn’t ours, I scoured social media and found it and got in touch with the photographer. And she reluctantly gave us permission to use it.”.

The photo went viral and became part of the story about the border crisis.

“AP benefits from having photo editors that are local to where the news is being produced,” indicates AP photographer Matt Rourke.

Industry observers note that “It’s a partnership,” adds Salinas. “The kind of partnership you lose when you sacrifice these jobs to save a few dollars.”.

Photo editors are intimately involved in the biggest stories of the day. They might be working closely with local photographers to move hundreds of shots illustrating crucial election results. Or securing the rights to sensitive images that convey difficult news. AP’s Pablo Salinas went in front of the camera to talk about the partnership that’s lost when news leaders sacrifice jobs like his. Tell the company their valuable work can’t just be done from anywhere at this link: https://t.co/euBigYM1tt.

— AP News Guild (@APNewsGuild) November 12, 2026.

An AP spokesperson tells TheWrap that the agency is respecting and following the collective bargaining agreement.

“This is part of the changes we announced over the summer to significantly scale our visual production capabilities at our new hub in Noida, India, where we have added dozens of talented journalists to our global news organization,” the spokesperson states.

The AP claims that its hub in Noida will soon employ nearly 100 video producers and photo editors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump declared the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

“This is a special structure,” Trump mentioned on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”.

In a recent development, it says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8.

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.

Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

It has been revealed that architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.

Recent findings suggest that “[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.

The ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s East Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.

It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history.

In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion mentioned it was “likely unlawful”.

Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.

The administration has also floated looks to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

Stedelijk Museum appoints Krist Gruijthuijsen as new director

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has revealed that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its upcoming director from July 2027.
  • Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he said he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.
  • “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has revealed that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its upcoming director from July 2027.

Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he said he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.

“The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”.

In a recent development, the Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.

Sources indicate that this success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.

But Gruijthuijsen noted he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he notes. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”.

Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.

According to recent reports, from one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental shows of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he indicates.

From the Finns, he will also bring an notable lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he claims: “Less talking, more doing.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thypoch has confirmed its first autofocus prime lens, the $349 AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor for Fujifilm X mount.
  • Editor’s Note: This article originally appeared on PetaPixel on October 27.
  • With its approximately 35mm equivalent focal length, Thypoch’s first autofocus lens for Fujifilm X mount and first autofocus prime lens period is well-suited to a wide range of photographic applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thypoch has confirmed its first autofocus prime lens, the $349 AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor for Fujifilm X mount.

Editor’s Note: This article originally appeared on PetaPixel on October 27. Multiple outlets including B&H Photo listed the lens, but Thypoch changed the release date after publication. As a courtesy, PetaPixel agreed to adjust the publish date to November 20. The content of this story is unchanged.

With its approximately 35mm equivalent focal length, Thypoch’s first autofocus lens for Fujifilm X mount and first autofocus prime lens period is well-suited to a wide range of photographic applications. The 35mm focal length is a classic one for a reason. It works well for street, landscapes, portraits, and travel, to name a few go-to genres.

It has been revealed that thypoch has long been associated with classically-inspired manual focus lenses, like the Simera 50mm f/1.4 and Ksana 21mm f/3.5. However, the manufacturer’s vibe changed considerably when it launched its first autofocus lens, the Voyager 24-50mm f/2.8 for full-frame Sony E-mount cameras.

Industry observers note that the new Thypoch AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor is styled much like the Voyager, with diagonal lines and a vintage-inspired yet modern design. Although beauty is subjective, the Sculptor will likely earn a few fans thanks to its handsome looks.

It's ultimately what's on the inside that counts, though. Inside the Sculptor, 12 lens elements are arranged across ten groups, promising edge-to-edge sharpness even at the maximum f/1.4 aperture. A 10-bladed aperture diaphragm sits behind the glass.

The lens is also quite compact, measuring just 71.4 millimeters (2.8 inches) long with a 52mm front filter thread. The lens weighs 283 grams (just under 10 ounces).

Industry observers note that the autofocus prime can focus as close as 0.25 meters (0.82 feet), giving a maximum magnification of about 0.13x. It's definitely not a macro lens.

According to recent reports, the Sculptor's most obvious competitor is Fujifilm's own XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WR lens, which costs $1,049.95. Fujifilm's lens weighs 375 grams (13.2 ounces) and is 77.8 millimeters (3.1 inches) long. Thypoch's latest lens is much lighter and more affordable.

Fujifilm XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WRBuy fresh on B&HFujifilm XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WRBuy used on KEH.comSigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN ContemporaryBuy new on B&HSigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN ContemporaryBuy used on KEH.com.

Industry observers note that another competitor is the Sigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN Contemporary. It's $609 right now thanks to a $50 discount and is generally well respected. It weighs 340 grams (12 ounces) and is 76.9 millimeters (three inches) long. Again, heavier than Thypoch's new lens by a decent margin.

Then there's the TTArtisan 23mm f/1.4 lens, which costs just $113.99. There's a massive catch, though, as TTArtisan's lens is manual focus only. It is extremely compact, measuring just 40.5 millimeters (1.6 inches) long. It weighs about 230 grams (8.1 ounces).

The Thypoch Sculptor AF 23mm f/1.4 should ship soon. It's available to preorder now for $349. It's the most affordable autofocus-equipped 23mm f/1.4 prime lens for Fujifilm X-mount cameras, and the lightest AF lens of its kind for the system. It will likely attract significant attention among Fujifilm camera owners.

Breaking: Drone Operator Films Manchester United Training Session and Leaks Video on YouTube

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A drone operator filmed English soccer team Manchester United’s first training session with new coach Mauricio Pochettino and shared the “unethical” footage on YouTube.
  • men’s national soccer team (USMNT) to become head coach of English Premier League club Manchester United.
  • According to recent reports, however, a drone operator who runs the YouTube account CC Overview — which describes itself as sharing “drone footage of construction at football stadia and events affecting our environment” — flew his aerial device over the facility during Pochettino’s first training session.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A drone operator filmed English soccer team Manchester United’s first training session with new coach Mauricio Pochettino and shared the “unethical” footage on YouTube.

Pochettino officially left the U.S. men’s national soccer team (USMNT) to become head coach of English Premier League club Manchester United. On Thursday, he oversaw his first training session with Man United’s first-team squad ahead of Sunday’s Premier League game against Liverpool at the club’s Carrington training ground.

According to recent reports, however, a drone operator who runs the YouTube account CC Overview — which describes itself as sharing “drone footage of construction at football stadia and events affecting our environment” — flew his aerial device over the facility during Pochettino’s first training session. He then posted a 12-minute segment on YouTube on Thursday.

In a recent development, according to a report by The Athletic, Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, were identifiable in the aerial footage, which amassed over 600,000 views on YouTube. The footage revealed Pochettino leading a training session with one group of players, while his assistant Jesus Perez oversaw two separate groups. The video, filmed at United’s Carrington training base, also captured audio of the YouTuber apparently controlling the drone saying “let’s get closer,” before zooming in on the new head coach.

Sources indicate that the drone operator has since apologized for a “total error in judgment.” He claims the aerial footage was legal under U.K. drone laws but has removed the “unethical” video from YouTube.

“A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Man United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part,” the drone operator writes in a post on YouTube.

Sources indicate that the drone operator describes aiming to film Pochettino in the club’s training kit for the first time, but adds he had no intention of recording a “meaningful training session.” The YouTuber claims he was operating under an incorrect assumption that it was open to media outlets. He also insists he acted independently and was not working on behalf of Liverpool or any other football club.

“I would like to apologize to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match,” the drone operator says.

Man United prohibits the use of drones at its Carrington training facility, where signs warn that anyone operating a drone could face civil action or prosecution.

In the U.K., capturing aerial footage using drones is permitted provided operators comply with Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) safety regulations, as well as privacy and data protection laws.

CAA guidance on privacy for drone use details: “If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you’re likely to be breaking data protection laws.” It adds that drone operators should “let people know before you start recording or taking pictures”.
